title: Rare Ventures Launches With $25 Million to Fund Treatments for Neglected Rare Diseases
excerpt: Backed by the Richard King Mellon Foundation, the Pittsburgh-based accelerator will invest in startups tackling seven rare conditions using a self-sustaining venture philanthropy model.
body:
• Pittsburgh-based Rare Ventures has launched with up to $25 million from the Richard King Mellon Foundation to invest in startups developing treatments for rare diseases.
  • The accelerator will initially target seven rare conditions, including epidermolysis bullosa and the neurodevelopmental disorder PACS1 syndrome.
  • Unlike traditional venture capital, Rare Ventures will reinvest all gains into new research rather than returning capital to investors, creating a self-sustaining funding model.
  • Partners include UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, Carnegie Mellon University, Stanford Medicine, and ElevateBio.

A new accelerator backed by one of America's oldest philanthropic foundations is taking aim at a stubborn problem in medicine: the thousands of rare diseases that have no approved treatment. Pittsburgh-based Rare Ventures has launched with up to $25 million from the Richard King Mellon Foundation, blending venture capital tactics with philanthropic goals to fund research into neglected disorders.

The model is straightforward but unusual. Like any venture investor, Rare Ventures will bet on high-growth biotech startups. But instead of returning profits to limited partners, all investment gains will be plowed back into new investments — creating what the organization hopes will be a perpetual funding engine for rare disease research.

From One Disease to Many

Rare Ventures extends the playbook of the EB Research Partnership, a New York-based nonprofit that funds research into epidermolysis bullosa, a group of genetic diseases that cause fragile, blistering skin. EB Research was co-founded in 2014 by Jill and Eddie Vedder, the Pearl Jam lead singer, after Jill Vedder befriended a family affected by the condition.

https://x.com/CarnegieMellon/status/2087565277630185926

Under CEO Michael Hund, EB Research pioneered the venture philanthropy approach with notable results. An $800,000 investment in Krystal Biotech shortly after its IPO in 2017 led to FDA approval for Vyjuvek in 2023 — the first approved treatment for any form of epidermolysis bullosa — and returned over $2 million to the nonprofit. A separate $500,000 investment linked to Stanford dermatology research generated a $3 million gain when Abeona Therapeutics secured FDA approval for another treatment, Zevaskyn, in 2025.

"The demand is there and we knew we had a model that could help many other rare diseases."

— Michael Hund, CEO, Rare Ventures and EB Research Partnership

Seven Diseases, One Model

Rare Ventures will initially focus on seven rare conditions, including epidermolysis bullosa, the neurodevelopmental disorder PACS1 syndrome, and LMNB1-related adult-onset autosomal dominant leukodystrophy, a neurodegenerative disease. A rare disease is defined as one affecting fewer than 200,000 people in the United States.

The scale of the unmet need is staggering. There are thousands of identified rare diseases, and the vast majority have no approved drug. "Clearly what we have to offer today is just not good enough," said Dr. Terence Dermody, chair of pediatrics at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and physician-in-chief at UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh.

An Institutional Network

Rare Ventures has assembled a network of academic and industry partners to support its portfolio companies. UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University provide research infrastructure, while Stanford University Medicine contributes clinical expertise. ElevateBio, a venture-backed company specializing in contract development and manufacturing for biotech firms, rounds out the partnership.

The approach differs from traditional rare disease nonprofits, which typically focus on a single condition. The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation and Breakthrough T1D (formerly the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation) have each created venture programs, but Rare Ventures' cross-disease model is designed to spread risk and capture efficiencies across multiple therapeutic areas.

Urgency and Ambition

"Many individuals afflicted by these rare diseases don't have time to wait," said Sam Reiman, director and trustee of the Richard King Mellon Foundation. The foundation, headquartered in Pittsburgh, is one of the largest philanthropic organizations in the United States, with a long history of supporting biomedical research in western Pennsylvania.

For Hund, who developed the venture philanthropy concept while pursuing his MBA at Yale School of Management, the expansion from EB Research to Rare Ventures represents the culmination of a decade-long strategy. The model's early returns suggest it can attract serious biotech talent and capital while keeping the mission squarely focused on patients — a combination that traditional drug development has struggled to achieve for diseases with small patient populations and limited commercial potential.
